claims.text: A combinatorial, high-throughput experimental approach integrated with data-driven machine-learning modeling can systematically reveal how varying Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr fractions affects mechanical properties.
The baseline material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The baseline alloy is consolidated by powder processing such as spark-plasma sintering or hot-isostatic pressing.
High-throughput synthesis of multiple composition variants is combined with machine-learning modeling of composition–mechanical-property relationships.
Each elemental content is varied incrementally by approximately ±5–10 at.% from the equiatomic composition.
Hardness, yield strength, and tensile strength are measured under identical processing and testing conditions.
Changing elemental fractions produces changes in localized atomic environments and lattice distortions.
Shifts in local chemical composition alter lattice strain.
Shifts in local chemical composition alter the potential for secondary-phase formation.
Changes in lattice strain and secondary-phase formation influence dislocation behavior and strengthening mechanisms.
Machine-learning predictions will identify composition ranges with yield-strength enhancements of up to 10–25% relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Prior reports place the yield strength of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 1000 MPa.
Large compositional deviations may induce secondary phases that complicate machine-learning predictions.
Extrapolation beyond ±10 at.% compositional shifts is uncertain.
It is unknown whether the predicted trends persist at elevated temperatures or far from the equiatomic composition.
